title_en: Shanghai Luwan District People's Procuratorate v. Wan Caihua — case of obstruction of testimony
ruling_gist_en: Where a perpetrator, for the purpose of evading debts, files a false civil lawsuit in collusion with others and instigates others to give false testimony, thereby obstructing the normal judicial activities of the people's court, the perpetrator shall be convicted and punished for the crime of obstructing testimony in accordance with Article 307 of the Criminal Law.

full_text_en:
Shanghai Luwan District People's Procuratorate v. Wan Caihua — crime of obstructing testimony

Ruling Summary

Where an actor, in order to evade debts, colludes with others to initiate a false civil lawsuit and instructs others to give false testimony, thereby obstructing the normal judicial activities of a people's court, the actor shall be convicted and punished for the crime of obstructing testimony in accordance with the provisions of Article 307 of the Criminal Law.

Prosecutorial Authority: Shanghai Luwan District People's Procuratorate.

Defendant: Wan Caihua, male, 49 years old, Han Chinese, university education, former staff member of Shanghai International Group, arrested in connection with this case on October 13, 2011.

The Shanghai Luwan District People's Procuratorate charged defendant Wan Caihua with the crime of obstructing testimony and initiated a public prosecution in the former Shanghai Luwan District People's Court. Subsequently, due to the merger and reorganization of Shanghai's administrative districts, this case was tried by the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court.

Charges in the Indictment: In October 2009, the defendant Wan Caihua, because others were demanding repayment of debts and in order to evade his obligation to repay debts in future litigation, fabricated in November of the same year the fact that he had borrowed RMB 3,000,000 from Han Bin (separately handled), instructed Han Bin to initiate a civil lawsuit in the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court as the plaintiff to recover the debt, and applied for property preservation. Through court mediation, a so-called agreement was reached. Later, the Pudong New Area People's Court verified that the lawsuit filed by Han Bin was a false lawsuit, and in August 2011, through retrial proceedings, issued a civil ruling permitting Han Bin to withdraw the lawsuit. After receiving a report, the public security organ investigated and apprehended Wan Caihua. Wan Caihua instructed others to give false testimony, with serious circumstances, and his conduct has constituted the crime of obstructing testimony, for which criminal liability shall be pursued according to law. Given that after his arrest he truthfully confessed the criminal facts, a lighter punishment may be imposed according to law.

The defendant Wan Caihua confessed to the facts charged in the indictment without reservation and stated in court that he had raised RMB 1,000,000 in cash and awaited the court's instructions for execution.

Defense counsel for the defendant Wan Caihua had no objection to the facts charged in the indictment but argued: first, that the obstruction of testimony by Wan Caihua involved a civil case and did not cause serious consequences, and that current laws and judicial interpretations have no clear provisions on what constitutes "serious circumstances" for this crime, thus objecting to the indictment's characterization of Wan Caihua's conduct as falling under "serious circumstances" as provided in Article 307, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Law; second, that the status of Han Bin in the false lawsuit was that of a plaintiff, not a witness, so Wan Caihua's act of instructing Han Bin to initiate the false lawsuit appears more consistent with the elements of the crime of aiding the fabrication of evidence. Given that Wan Caihua truthfully confessed the criminal facts after his arrest and that the circumstances of the crime were minor, defense counsel recommended that the court exempt him from criminal punishment.

The Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court found through trial:

In October 2009, the defendant Wan Caihua, knowing that others were demanding repayment of debts and had already initiated a civil lawsuit against him in court, and in order to evade his obligation to repay the debts after losing the case, fabricated in November of the same year the fact that he had borrowed RMB 3,000,000 from Han Bin (separately handled), instructed Han Bin to initiate a civil lawsuit in the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court as the plaintiff to recover the debt, and applied for property preservation. Subsequently, through court mediation, Han Bin and Wan Caihua reached a so-called mediation agreement, and the court issued a civil mediation document establishing the creditor-debtor relationship between them.

It was also found that after the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court verified that the case of Han Bin v. defendant Wan Caihua concerning a private loan was a false lawsuit, it initiated retrial proceedings in July 2011. During the retrial, Han Bin submitted an application to withdraw the lawsuit, and Wan Caihua had no objection. Accordingly, the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court lawfully issued a civil ruling, revoking the original civil mediation document and permitting Han Bin to withdraw the lawsuit. After filing the case and conducting an investigation, the public security organ apprehended Wan Caihua on May 10, 2011.

The above facts are fully confirmed by evidence including the testimony and written statement of Han Bin, the civil complaint, application for litigation preservation, civil ruling, interview record, civil mediation document issued by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court, and the work record issued by the Luwan Branch of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau.

The Core Issue at First Instance in this Case: Whether the conduct of the defendant Wan Caihua in colluding with others to carry out a false lawsuit constitutes the crime of obstructing testimony, and if so, whether it falls under the "serious circumstances" as provided in Article 307, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Law.

First Instance Judgment of the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court:

The motive of the defendant Wan Caihua in colluding with Han Bin to carry out a false lawsuit was to evade the huge debts he owed to others. The specific method was to collude with Han Bin, fabricate the fact that he had borrowed money from Han Bin, forge corresponding evidence, and then instruct Han Bin to file a lawsuit in court. The ultimate result he sought was to have the case concluded through court mediation, confirming the debt relationship between him and Han Bin, thereby transferring the "owed" RMB 3,000,000 in full to Han, creating the false impression that he had no capacity to repay debts, and using this to deny and evade his huge debts to others. Wan Caihua clearly knew that his conduct would infringe upon the legitimate rights and interests of creditors, disrupt the normal judicial work order and judicial credibility, yet he actively pursued this outcome. His conduct clearly has social harmfulness and criminal punishability and also meets the elements of the crime under Chapter Six, "Crimes of Obstructing Justice," of the Specific Provisions of the Criminal Law.

According to the provisions of Article 307, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Law, the crime of obstructing testimony refers to acts of preventing witnesses from giving testimony or instructing others to give false testimony by means of violence, threats, bribery, etc. The phrase "instructing others to give false testimony" cannot be narrowly interpreted as only instructing witnesses to give false testimony; rather, it means instructing any person, including witnesses, parties, expert witnesses, notaries, interpreters, and others, who may present evidence or provide leads to evidence during the litigation process. Likewise, "false testimony" cannot be narrowly understood as only false witness testimony; it includes all evidentiary materials, including oral evidence, documentary evidence, physical evidence, expert conclusions, etc. Based on the facts of this case, the defendant Wan Caihua instructed Han Bin to file a false civil lawsuit in court, provide false evidence, and make false statements. It can be determined that the above conduct of Wan Caihua falls within "instructing others to give false testimony" and fully meets the elements of the crime of obstructing testimony. Defense counsel's opinion that Wan Caihua's conduct does not constitute the crime of obstructing testimony but constitutes the crime of aiding the fabrication of evidence cannot be sustained.

Defense counsel argued that Wan Caihua's obstruction of testimony involved a civil case and did not cause serious consequences, and that current laws and judicial interpretations have no clear provisions on what constitutes "serious circumstances" for this crime, thus objecting to the indictment's characterization of Wan Caihua's conduct as falling under "serious circumstances" as provided in Article 307, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Law. Regarding this, the court held that, based on the facts of this case, Wan Caihua instructed others to give false testimony and carried out a false lawsuit. This not only showed malicious intent to evade huge debts but also seriously infringed upon the work order of judicial organs and caused great damage to judicial credibility. His conduct falls under the "serious circumstances" as provided in Article 307, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Law.

In summary, the conduct of the defendant Wan Caihua constitutes the crime of obstructing testimony, with serious circumstances. Given that Wan Caihua truthfully confessed his crimes after his arrest and showed a relatively good attitude of admitting guilt, a lighter punishment may be imposed according to law. Pursuant to Article 307, paragraph 1 and Article 67, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Law of the PRC, the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court rendered the following judgment on October 18, 2011:

Defendant Wan Caihua is convicted of the crime of obstructing testimony and sentenced to three years' imprisonment.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, the defendant Wan Caihua did not file an appeal within the statutory period, and the first-instance judgment has taken legal effect.
